title: 7 signs your CV is the reason you’re not getting interviews
cover_alt: Woman planning her next career move with sticky notes on a wall
excerpt: If you’re qualified, applying often and still hearing nothing back, the problem may not be you. It may be the two pages standing in for you.
seo_title: 7 signs your CV is why you’re not getting interviews
seo_description: Applying often but hearing nothing back? Here are 7 signs your CV, not your experience, is the reason you’re not getting interviews in Nigeria.
author: Dé Pitch Team
bridge: Every CV needs a different fix, and yours depends on your field and the roles you’re targeting. That’s what we work through in a free consultation, and in a full CV revamp if you need one.

faq.q: How do I know if my CV is the problem or the job market?
faq.a: If you’re applying to roles you’re genuinely qualified for and getting no responses at all, not even rejections, the CV is usually the first place to look. A tough market slows replies down. It rarely stops them completely.

faq.q: How many applications should it take to get an interview?
faq.a: There’s no fixed number, and it varies by industry and level. But if you’ve sent dozens of tailored applications for suitable roles and heard nothing, treat that as a signal, not bad luck.

faq.q: Can a CV be too long?
faq.a: Yes. Length itself isn’t the issue; relevance is. A long CV that buries your strongest work is harder to read than a short one that leads with it.

faq.q: Should I use a CV template from the internet?
faq.a: Templates aren’t the problem, but many popular designs use columns, icons and graphics that application tracking systems struggle to read. Looking good to a human and being readable by software are two different tests.

body:
If you’re qualified, applying regularly and still hearing nothing back, your CV is very often the reason. Not your experience. Not your degree. Not the economy. The two pages that are supposed to represent you might simply be telling the wrong story, or telling it in a way nobody gets to read.

Recruiters and hiring managers skim. Software screens before people do. Somewhere between “submit” and “we’d like to invite you”, a lot of good candidates quietly disappear. Here are seven signs it’s happening to you.

## 1. You’re getting silence, not rejections

Rejection emails are annoying, but they mean someone looked. Total silence across dozens of applications usually means your CV isn’t making it past the first filter, whether that’s a person skimming for ten seconds or a system scanning for keywords.

If your inbox is quieter than your group chat on a Monday morning, that’s a sign.

## 2. You send the same CV to every job

One CV for a bank, a fintech startup and an NGO feels efficient. It isn’t. Each of those employers is scanning for different words, different results and a different kind of person.

A CV that tries to fit every role usually ends up fitting none of them.

## 3. It reads like a job description, not a highlight reel

“Responsible for managing social media accounts.” “Duties included preparing reports.”

That tells a recruiter what your job was supposed to be. It doesn’t tell them what you actually did, how well you did it, or why it mattered. When every line starts with “responsible for”, your CV sounds like everybody else’s.

## 4. Your best work is on page two

The top third of your first page does most of the work. If your proudest achievement, your most relevant role or the skill that makes you right for this job is hiding further down, a busy reader may never get there.

Ask yourself honestly: if someone only read the top of your CV, would they want to keep reading?

## 5. It looks great, but software can’t read it

Two columns, icons for your phone number, skill bars, a photo in a circle. It looks modern. But many companies, especially larger ones, use applicant tracking systems that scan CVs before a human ever sees them, and heavily designed layouts can confuse them.

Your CV has two audiences: a machine and a person. It needs to pass both.

## 6. You’re getting interviews for the wrong jobs

This one is sneaky. You are getting calls, just not for the roles you want. That usually means your CV is positioning you for the job you have, or had, instead of the job you’re going after.

If you want to move up, move across or change industries, your CV has to make that move first.

## 7. You can’t explain your CV in one sentence

Try it. “I’m a ___ who ___.” If you can’t say what your CV is selling in one line, a recruiter can’t either. Clarity is the difference between “interesting candidate” and “next”.

## So what now?

If three or more of these sound familiar, it’s not you, and you don’t need to apply to a hundred more jobs. You need a CV that tells the right story for the roles you actually want.

The tricky part is that there’s no single fix. A CV for a graduate trainee role in Lagos looks nothing like one for a remote product role paying in dollars. What works depends on your field, your level and where you’re aiming next.

title: Would you take ₦1.2m to work somewhere you hate?
cover_alt: Man thinking at his laptop late in the evening
excerpt: On paper, ₦1.2 million a month is an easy yes. In real life, it’s one of the most honest questions about work you can ask yourself.
seo_title: Would you take ₦1.2m a month at a job you hate?
seo_description: ₦1.2m somewhere you hate or ₦700k somewhere you enjoy? An honest look at money, toxic workplaces and how long is too long to stay.
author: Dé Pitch Team
bridge: There’s no universal right answer here. Yours depends on your bills, your plans and how much the job is really costing you. If you’re stuck between the money and your peace, that’s exactly the kind of decision we work through, one to one, in a free consultation.

faq.q: Is it okay to take a job just for the money?
faq.a: Yes. Lots of people take a role mainly for the salary, and that can be a smart, deliberate choice. It works best when you know why you’re there, what you’re building with the money, and roughly when you plan to leave.

faq.q: How do I know if a job is toxic or just hard?
faq.a: Hard jobs stretch you; toxic ones shrink you. If the work is demanding but you’re learning and respected, that’s hard. If you dread going in, feel constantly undermined or your health is slipping, take that seriously.

faq.q: How long should I stay in a job I don’t like?
faq.a: There’s no fixed rule. Many people find it helps to set a clear goal, like a savings target, a skill or a date, so staying feels like a plan rather than being stuck.

body:
Okay, let’s settle this. Would you take ₦1.2 million a month to work somewhere you absolutely hate?

For most people, the honest answer is: it depends. On your rent. On your family. On how bad “hate” really is. And on how long you’d have to stay. That’s what makes it one of the most revealing questions you can ask about work.

## Why ₦1.2m is an easy yes on paper

Let’s not pretend money doesn’t matter. ₦1.2 million a month can change a lot.

- Bills get paid on time, every time.
- Savings start to look like actual savings.
- Maybe you finally move out.
- Maybe you help your family without panicking about your own month.

Anyone who tells you to “just choose happiness” has probably never had to choose between rent and peace of mind. Money buys options, and options are a kind of freedom.

## So what’s the problem?

The problem is that you spend most of your waking life at work.

If you hate being there, the salary slowly starts to feel less like a reward and more like compensation for suffering. The Sunday-night dread. The meetings you leave feeling smaller. The tiredness that has nothing to do with how much you actually worked.

That cost doesn’t show up on your payslip, but you pay it anyway.

## ₦1.2m and miserable, or ₦700k and okay?

Here’s where it gets interesting. Put a second option on the table: ₦700k at a place you genuinely enjoy. Good manager, decent team, work that makes sense.

Some people would take the ₦700k without blinking. Others would take the ₦1.2m and not feel bad about it at all. Neither choice is more ambitious or more mature. They’re just different trade-offs, made by people in different seasons of life.

> Taking the money doesn’t mean you’ve chosen the job forever.

## The better question: how long are you willing to stay?

Maybe the real question isn’t “would you take it?” Maybe it’s “for how long?”

Six months? A year? Until you’ve saved enough to leave? Until you’ve learnt the skill that gets you the next role?

There’s a big difference between staying somewhere hard with a plan and staying somewhere hard because you’re scared there’s nothing better out there. The first is a strategy. The second is a trap that looks like a salary.

## Signs the money has stopped being worth it

- You dread every Sunday evening, not just some of them.
- Your health, sleep or relationships are clearly taking the hit.
- You’re not learning anything you’d want on your next CV.
- You’ve stopped imagining any other version of your working life.

If that list feels uncomfortably familiar, the number on your payslip may be costing you more than it pays.

## So, what’s your pick?

₦1.2 million at a job you hate, or ₦700k somewhere you actually enjoy? Tell us in the comments on Instagram or LinkedIn. We read them all, and we’re genuinely curious where the Pitch Club lands on this one.

title: Why your job adverts attract the wrong candidates
cover_alt: Team of professionals gathered around a desk
excerpt: Hundreds of applications and nobody you’d actually hire? The problem often starts before the first CV arrives: in the advert itself.
seo_title: Why your job adverts attract the wrong candidates
seo_description: Getting lots of applicants but few good ones? The reasons small and growing businesses in Nigeria attract the wrong candidates, starting with the job advert.
author: Dé Pitch Team
bridge: Every role needs a different search, and the right hire depends on your team, your budget and your culture. That’s what we work out with you before we shortlist anyone.

faq.q: Why do I get so many unqualified applicants?
faq.a: Usually because the advert makes it easy for anyone to apply and hard for the right person to recognise themselves. Vague requirements and generic descriptions widen the funnel in the wrong direction.

faq.q: Should I put the salary in a job advert?
faq.a: Many employers find that a salary range filters out people with very different expectations and saves time for both sides. Whether it suits your business depends on your sector and your pay structure.

faq.q: How long should a job advert be?
faq.a: Long enough to explain the role, the must-haves and why someone should want to join you, and short enough to read on a phone. Most candidates will see it on mobile first.

faq.q: When should I use a recruitment agency?
faq.a: Agencies are most useful when a role is hard to fill, important to get right, or when your team doesn’t have time to screen properly. A bad hire usually costs far more than the search.

body:
If your job advert brings in hundreds of applications and almost nobody you’d actually hire, the advert is usually doing part of the damage. It’s not that good candidates don’t exist. It’s that your advert isn’t speaking to them, or it’s speaking to everybody at once.

For small and growing businesses, that’s expensive. Every hour spent reading the wrong CVs is an hour not spent running the business. And every rushed hire you make because you’re tired of searching costs even more.

Here’s why it happens.

## The job title says one thing, the job is another

“Admin Officer” can mean receptionist, office manager, personal assistant or all three. When the title is vague, candidates fill in the gaps with their own assumptions, and you get applications from people imagining a completely different job.

The right people need to recognise themselves in the first five words.

## Everything is “required”

Ten years of experience, five software tools, a master’s degree and “ability to work under pressure”, for a mid-level role. Long wish lists do two things: they scare off capable people who don’t tick every box, and they barely slow down people who apply to everything regardless.

If everything is a must-have, nothing is.

## It describes duties, not the actual work

“Handle client relations. Prepare reports. Other duties as assigned.” That could be any company in Nigeria. Strong candidates want to know what a normal week looks like, what problems they’ll be solving, and what success looks like after six months.

When the advert can’t answer that, the best people scroll past.

## It never says why anyone should want to join

Good candidates usually have options. Your advert is competing with every other company hiring for the same skills, so it needs to sell a little, too. Who will they work with? What will they learn? What’s different about working with you?

An advert that only lists demands reads like a company that only takes.

## Nothing about pay, hours or location

Remote, hybrid or on-site? Lagos Island or the mainland? A salary range or “competitive”? When the basics are missing, people apply first and ask questions later, and you find out in the interview that they were never going to accept.

## The wrong channels for the right people

Where you post decides who sees it. The candidates you want may not be scrolling the same job boards and WhatsApp groups as everyone else. Some of the best people aren’t actively looking at all.

## The real cost of the wrong candidates

It’s not just time spent screening. It’s the interviews that go nowhere, the offer that gets declined, and the hire who leaves after three months, so you’re back at the start, only more tired.

Getting the advert right is the first step. Getting the right people to see it, and assessing them properly once they apply, is where the real work starts.
